title: 🔦 Light & Shadow Lab
description: Welcome to the Light & Shadow Lab! You are a Grade 6 student exploring the amazing world of light and optics. Over 14 weeks, you will discover how light travels, creates shadows, bounces off mirrors, bends through lenses, and splits into a rainbow of colors. Experiment with torches, mirrors, prisms, and lenses while keeping your lab safe and your curiosity alive. Can you master optics and create a dazzling light show for the Science Fair?
subject: physics
how_to_play: You are a Grade 6 student exploring light and optics over a 14-week science lab program.
Each week presents an optics challenge with choices that affect your knowledge, safety, and creativity.
Watch your dashboard — your Lab Stations (Optics Bench, Shadow Studio, Mirror Station, Lens Lab, Color Lab) are interconnected.
NPCs like Dr. Prism (teacher), Lumina (light mascot), Aisha, and Dev react to your decisions.
Random events like bulb burnouts and visiting scientists will test your adaptability.
Keep your Safety Rating high — if it drops too low, you will lose access to the laser equipment!
learning_objectives: Understand that light travels in straight lines (rectilinear propagation)
Learn how shadows are formed and what affects their size and shape
Explore the law of reflection and how mirrors work
Discover refraction — how light bends when passing through different materials
Understand how lenses focus and spread light (convex and concave)
Learn how white light splits into colors through a prism (dispersion)
cultural_context: School science laboratory, hands-on STEM learning, light and optics exploration

rounds.round_title: Week 1: Welcome to the World of Light
rounds.situation: It is your first day in the optics lab! The benches are covered with torches, mirrors, prisms, and colorful filters. Dr. Prism welcomes the class and says: 'Before we start any experiments, let us understand what light is and how to stay safe around bright sources.' A beam of sunlight streams through the window, casting a bright rectangle on the floor. How do you want to start?
rounds.goal: Choose how to begin your light and optics education.
rounds.coaching_moment: Delayed gratification: Spending time on fundamentals now will make every future experiment easier and safer.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Why is it important to understand light safety rules before starting hands-on experiments?
rounds.image_prompt: Grade 6 students entering a bright optics lab for the first time, lab benches with mirrors and prisms, sunlight streaming through windows, excited faces, Dr. Prism at whiteboard

choices.label: A. The Sun, stars, and fireflies are luminous objects because they produce their own light
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ Luminous objects are those that produce their own light. The Sun is a natural luminous source, and fireflies produce light through a chemical reaction called bioluminescence. Without luminous objects, we would not be able to see anything at all!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Weighing multiple outcomes before deciding strengthens your planning skills.

choices.label: B. The Moon is a luminous object because it shines brightly at night
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 The Moon looks bright, but it does NOT produce its own light. It is a non-luminous object that reflects sunlight. Think of it like a mirror in the sky — it bounces the Sun's light toward Earth. That is why the Moon has phases depending on how much sunlight hits it!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Looking beyond the obvious choice shows you think strategically.

choices.label: C. A mirror is a luminous object because you can see light coming from it
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 A mirror does not produce its own light — it only reflects light from other sources. That makes it a non-luminous object. The key test is: does the object CREATE light on its own? If you put a mirror in a completely dark room with no light source, you would see nothing in it!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Planning your approach carefully is a sign of strategic reasoning.

choices.label: D. All objects that we can see are luminous objects
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 We can see most objects around us (books, desks, walls) even though they do not produce light. These are non-luminous objects — we see them because they reflect light from luminous sources like the Sun or a lamp. Only a small number of objects actually produce their own light!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Thinking ahead about consequences shows strategic planning ability.

rounds.round_title: Week 2: Light Sources All Around Us
rounds.situation: This week Dr. Prism brings out a collection of light sources — a torch, a candle, an LED bulb, a glow stick, and even a jar of fireflies! 'Light comes from many sources,' she explains. 'Some make their own light (luminous objects) and others reflect light from somewhere else (non-luminous objects). Let us explore the difference!' Aisha is fascinated by the fireflies.
rounds.goal: Classify objects as luminous and non-luminous, and explore different light sources.
rounds.coaching_moment: Strategic thinking: Careful observation and classification are the first steps in any scientific investigation.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Is the Moon a luminous or non-luminous object? How do you know?
rounds.image_prompt: Lab bench with various light sources lined up — lit candle, torch, LED bulb, glow stick, jar of fireflies — student classifying them in a notebook, warm lighting

choices.label: A. Light always travels in straight lines, which is why shadows have sharp edges
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ Light travels in straight lines — this is called rectilinear propagation. Because light cannot bend around objects on its own, when an opaque object blocks the light, a dark area (shadow) forms behind it with clear edges. This is also why you cannot see around corners!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Considering long-term impact before acting builds strategic thinking.

choices.label: B. Light travels in curved paths, which is why we can see around corners
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 Light does NOT naturally curve around corners — it travels in straight lines. That is exactly why you cannot see someone standing behind a wall. If light could bend around objects freely, there would be no shadows at all! We need mirrors or lenses to redirect light.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Weighing multiple outcomes before deciding strengthens your planning skills.

choices.label: C. Shadows are formed because light passes through all objects equally
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 Shadows form precisely because light CANNOT pass through opaque objects. When an opaque object (like your body) blocks the straight-line path of light, the area behind it receives no light and appears dark — that is a shadow. Different materials let different amounts of light through!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Looking beyond the obvious choice shows you think strategically.

choices.label: D. Light can only travel when there is air to carry it, like sound
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 Unlike sound, light does NOT need air or any material to travel through. Light can travel through the vacuum of space — that is how sunlight reaches Earth across 150 million kilometers of empty space! Sound needs a medium (air, water, solid), but light does not.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Planning your approach carefully is a sign of strategic reasoning.

rounds.situation: Dr. Prism darkens the room and turns on a single bright lamp. 'Watch this,' she says, placing objects between the lamp and the wall. Sharp shadows appear! 'Shadows prove that light travels in straight lines. But why are some shadows sharp and others fuzzy? Why do shadows change size?' She hands you a torch, some cardboard cutouts, and a white screen. Time to investigate!
rounds.goal: Understand how shadows are formed and what affects their size and sharpness.
rounds.coaching_moment: Adaptability: Science often gives surprising results. Being willing to change your thinking when evidence contradicts your expectations is key.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Why is your shadow longer in the morning and evening but shorter at noon?
rounds.image_prompt: Darkened lab room with a bright lamp casting sharp shadows of cardboard shapes on a white screen, student moving objects between light and screen, dramatic shadow play

choices.label: A. A shadow gets bigger when the object is moved closer to the light source
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ When an object moves closer to the light source, it blocks a wider cone of light rays, creating a larger shadow on the screen. Moving it away from the light (closer to the screen) makes the shadow smaller. This is how shadow puppet artists control the size of their puppets on screen!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Thinking ahead about consequences shows strategic planning ability.

choices.label: B. Shadows are always the exact same size as the object creating them
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 Shadow size depends on the position of the object between the light source and the screen. A small toy held close to a lamp can cast a shadow much bigger than itself! The closer the object is to the light, the larger the shadow. Try it yourself with a torch and your hand.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Considering long-term impact before acting builds strategic thinking.

choices.label: C. Colored objects create colored shadows
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 Shadows are always dark (usually black or grey) regardless of the color of the object. A shadow is simply the absence of light in an area — the blocked light never reaches the screen. A red ball and a blue ball of the same size will create identical dark shadows!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Weighing multiple outcomes before deciding strengthens your planning skills.

choices.label: D. Transparent objects like clear glass create the darkest shadows
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 Transparent objects like clear glass let most light pass through, so they create very faint shadows or almost no shadow at all. The darkest shadows are created by opaque objects (like wood, metal, or cardboard) that block light completely. Translucent objects create partial, fuzzy shadows.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Looking beyond the obvious choice shows you think strategically.

rounds.situation: Dr. Prism brings out a collection of mirrors — flat, curved, and even a fun-house mirror! 'When light hits a smooth surface, it bounces back in a predictable way,' she explains. 'The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection. This is the Law of Reflection!' She draws a diagram on the board. Dev wants to measure angles precisely while Aisha is fascinated by the fun-house mirror distortions.
rounds.goal: Master the Law of Reflection and understand how mirrors work.
rounds.coaching_moment: Ethical reasoning: Accurate measurement and honest data recording are the foundation of all science. Never change your data to match what you expected!
rounds.reflection_prompt: Why do ambulances have AMBULANCE written backwards on the front? How does reflection explain this?
rounds.image_prompt: Student carefully measuring angle of incidence and reflection on a flat mirror using a protractor, ray of light from torch visible, lab bench with multiple mirrors

choices.label: A. When light hits a smooth mirror, the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ The Law of Reflection states that the angle at which light hits a surface (angle of incidence) is always equal to the angle at which it bounces off (angle of reflection). Both angles are measured from the 'normal' — an imaginary line perpendicular to the mirror. This is why mirrors create clear, predictable images!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Planning your approach carefully is a sign of strategic reasoning.

choices.label: B. Light always reflects straight back the way it came, no matter what angle it hits the mirror
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 Light only bounces straight back if it hits the mirror at exactly 90 degrees (perpendicular). At any other angle, it bounces off at the SAME angle on the other side of the normal line. If you shine a torch at a mirror from the left, the reflected beam goes to the right. Try it!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Thinking ahead about consequences shows strategic planning ability.

choices.label: C. Rough surfaces like walls do not reflect any light at all
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 Rough surfaces DO reflect light — that is actually how we see them! But they reflect light in many different random directions (called diffuse reflection or irregular reflection). Smooth surfaces like mirrors reflect light in one organized direction (regular reflection), creating clear images.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Considering long-term impact before acting builds strategic thinking.

choices.label: D. The image in a plane mirror is always smaller than the actual object
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 A plane (flat) mirror creates an image that is the SAME size as the object. It is also the same distance behind the mirror as the object is in front. The image is laterally inverted though — your left hand appears as a right hand. That is why 'AMBULANCE' is written backwards on ambulances!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Weighing multiple outcomes before deciding strengthens your planning skills.

rounds.situation: Dr. Prism places a pencil in a glass of water and asks: 'Why does the pencil look broken at the water surface?' The class murmurs. 'This is refraction — light changes direction when it passes from one material to another, like air to water or air to glass,' she explains. 'Today we explore why light bends and how much!' She sets out glass blocks, water tanks, and ray boxes.
rounds.goal: Understand refraction and why light bends when entering a new medium.
rounds.coaching_moment: Strategic thinking: Refraction is a powerful concept. Once you understand it, you can explain rainbows, mirages, and why swimming pools look shallower than they are!
rounds.reflection_prompt: Why does a swimming pool look shallower than it actually is? How does refraction explain this?
rounds.image_prompt: Student shining a ray of light through a glass block, visible bending of the light ray at the surface, protractor measuring angles, lab bench with water tank and prisms

choices.label: A. Light bends when it passes from air into water because it slows down in water
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ Refraction happens because light travels at different speeds in different materials. Light is fastest in air and slows down in denser materials like water or glass. When it slows down, it bends toward the 'normal' line. This is why a pencil looks broken when half-dipped in water — the light from the underwater part bends as it exits the water!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Looking beyond the obvious choice shows you think strategically.

choices.label: B. Light travels at the same speed in all materials, so it never changes direction
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 Light actually travels at DIFFERENT speeds in different materials. It is fastest in vacuum and air (~300,000 km/s) and slower in water and glass. This speed change causes the light to bend (refract) at the boundary between two materials. Thats why a swimming pool looks shallower than it really is!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Planning your approach carefully is a sign of strategic reasoning.

choices.label: C. A pencil in water looks broken because the water pushes it into a bent shape
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 The pencil is NOT actually bending — it is perfectly straight! It only LOOKS broken because the light rays from the underwater part of the pencil bend (refract) when they pass from water to air before reaching your eyes. Your brain assumes light travels in straight lines, so it sees the underwater part in the wrong position.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Thinking ahead about consequences shows strategic planning ability.

choices.label: D. Refraction only happens with very hot light sources like the Sun
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 Refraction happens with ALL light, regardless of temperature or source. A torch, a candle, or even moonlight will refract when passing from air to water or glass. Refraction depends on the change in the material light passes through, not the type of light source.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Considering long-term impact before acting builds strategic thinking.

widget_answer.prompt: Light hits a mirror at 30 degrees. What is the angle of reflection?

rounds.situation: Dr. Prism hands out two types of lenses: convex (thick in the middle) and concave (thin in the middle). 'Lenses are everywhere — in your eyes, cameras, telescopes, and microscopes,' she says. 'Today we explore how lenses bend light to focus or spread it.' She asks each team to find the focal length of their convex lens by focusing sunlight onto a piece of paper. Dev is carefully measuring while Aisha is amazed by the tiny bright dot of focused sunlight.
rounds.goal: Understand how convex and concave lenses work and find their focal lengths.
rounds.coaching_moment: Creativity: True creativity is not random — it combines knowledge, imagination, and the courage to try something new with lenses.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Why do people who are nearsighted need concave lenses, while farsighted people need convex lenses?
rounds.image_prompt: Student holding a convex lens in sunlight, focusing a bright spot of light onto white paper, another student measuring focal length with a ruler, lab bench with assorted lenses

choices.label: A. A convex lens is thicker in the middle and converges (focuses) light rays to a point
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ A convex lens bulges outward (thicker in the middle) and bends light inward, focusing parallel light rays to a single point called the focal point. This is how magnifying glasses work — and how the lens in your eye focuses images onto your retina so you can see clearly!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Weighing multiple outcomes before deciding strengthens your planning skills.

choices.label: B. A concave lens focuses light rays to a single bright point
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 A concave lens is thinner in the middle and SPREADS light rays apart (diverges them) — the opposite of focusing! It is the CONVEX lens that focuses light to a point. Concave lenses are used in glasses for nearsighted (myopic) people to spread the light before it enters the eye.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Looking beyond the obvious choice shows you think strategically.

choices.label: C. Lenses work by reflecting light, just like mirrors
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 Lenses and mirrors work in completely different ways. Mirrors REFLECT light (bounce it back), while lenses REFRACT light (bend it as it passes through). Light actually travels THROUGH a lens, changing direction as it enters and exits the glass. Both are useful in optics but for different reasons!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Planning your approach carefully is a sign of strategic reasoning.

choices.label: D. All lenses are the same — they only come in one shape
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 Lenses come in two main types: convex (thicker in the middle, focuses light) and concave (thinner in the middle, spreads light). They have opposite effects! Cameras, telescopes, and microscopes use combinations of both types to create sharp, magnified images.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Thinking ahead about consequences shows strategic planning ability.

challenge.question: Light travels at 300,000 km/s. How far does it travel in 2 seconds? (in km)

rounds.situation: EMERGENCY! When you arrive at the lab this morning, disaster has struck. Over the weekend, a shelf collapsed and many of the lab's best mirrors and lenses crashed to the floor. Shattered glass is everywhere, the expensive concave mirror is cracked, and two prisms are chipped beyond use. Dr. Prism is visibly upset but stays professional: 'Safety first — nobody touches the broken glass. Now, how do we continue learning with limited equipment?'
rounds.goal: Handle the equipment crisis safely and find ways to continue learning with limited resources.
rounds.coaching_moment: Resilience: Emergencies test your character. Staying calm, following procedures, and learning from setbacks are what separate good scientists from frustrated ones.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Can limitations actually make you MORE creative? Think of an example from your own life.
rounds.image_prompt: Science lab with broken mirrors and cracked lenses on the floor, shelf collapsed, caution tape around the area, worried students and calm teacher, safety gloves visible

choices.label: A. An image in a plane mirror is the same size as the object, at the same distance behind the mirror, and laterally inverted
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ A plane mirror creates a virtual image that is the same size as the object, appears to be the same distance behind the mirror as the object is in front, and is laterally inverted (left and right are swapped). That is why when you raise your right hand, your mirror image raises its left hand!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Considering long-term impact before acting builds strategic thinking.

choices.label: B. The image in a plane mirror is upside down and magnified
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 The image in a flat (plane) mirror is NOT upside down and NOT magnified — it is the same size and upright. It IS laterally inverted though (left-right swapped). Concave mirrors can create upside-down or magnified images, but flat mirrors always produce same-size, upright, laterally inverted images.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Weighing multiple outcomes before deciding strengthens your planning skills.

choices.label: C. Mirror images are real images that can be projected onto a screen
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 Images in plane mirrors are VIRTUAL images, not real images. A virtual image cannot be caught on a screen because the light rays do not actually meet behind the mirror — they only APPEAR to come from behind it. Real images (like those from a projector) can be caught on a screen because light rays actually converge there.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Looking beyond the obvious choice shows you think strategically.

choices.label: D. If you stand 2 meters from a mirror, your image appears 4 meters behind the mirror
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 In a plane mirror, the image distance equals the object distance. So if you stand 2 meters in front of the mirror, your image appears 2 meters behind it — making you appear 4 meters away from yourself, but only 2 meters behind the mirror. The mirror does not double the distance behind it!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Planning your approach carefully is a sign of strategic reasoning.

rounds.situation: With some equipment replaced and improvised substitutes ready, Dr. Prism introduces a new investigation: 'Why can you see through glass but not through wood? Why does frosted glass blur your view?' She sets out samples of transparent (clear glass, water), translucent (wax paper, frosted glass), and opaque (cardboard, metal) materials. 'Classify these and explain WHY light behaves differently with each.'
rounds.goal: Classify materials by how they interact with light and understand why.
rounds.coaching_moment: Strategic thinking: Classifying materials by their optical properties is how engineers choose materials for windows, lampshades, and privacy screens.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Why are bathroom windows often made of frosted glass instead of clear glass?
rounds.image_prompt: Lab bench with rows of materials — clear glass, frosted glass, wax paper, cardboard, fabric — with a torch shining through each, student observing and classifying

choices.label: A. Frosted glass is translucent — it lets some light through but scatters it, so objects look blurry
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ Translucent materials like frosted glass, butter paper, and thin fabric let some light pass through but scatter it in random directions. This means you can tell there is light on the other side, but you cannot see clear shapes. That is why bathroom windows are often frosted — they let in light while keeping privacy!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Thinking ahead about consequences shows strategic planning ability.

choices.label: B. Translucent objects block all light completely, just like opaque objects
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 Translucent objects do NOT block all light — they let SOME light through but scatter it. That is the key difference from opaque objects (which block all light). Hold a piece of wax paper up to a light — you will see a glow but not clear shapes. An opaque cardboard would show nothing at all!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Considering long-term impact before acting builds strategic thinking.

choices.label: C. Clear glass is opaque because you can see your reflection in it
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 Clear glass is TRANSPARENT, not opaque. Transparent materials let light pass through clearly so you can see objects on the other side. The reflection you sometimes see in glass is just a small amount of light bouncing off the surface — most of the light passes right through!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Weighing multiple outcomes before deciding strengthens your planning skills.

choices.label: D. Wood can become transparent if you polish it enough
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 Polishing an opaque material like wood makes it smoother and shinier, but it does not make it transparent. The material's atomic structure determines whether light can pass through it. Glass is transparent because its molecules are arranged in a way that light can travel through. Wood's molecules absorb and block light regardless of surface smoothness.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Looking beyond the obvious choice shows you think strategically.

widget_answer.prompt: If the angle of incidence is 45 degrees, what is the angle of refraction in the same medium?

rounds.situation: Dr. Prism challenges the class: 'Can you see around corners? Submarines do it. Soldiers in trenches did it. Today you will build your own periscope using mirrors and cardboard tubes!' She shows a diagram of how two angled mirrors inside a tube let you see over walls and around obstacles. Dev immediately starts calculating mirror angles while Aisha imagines spying on the teachers' lounge!
rounds.goal: Design and build a working periscope using reflection principles.
rounds.coaching_moment: Creativity: Engineering is applied science. When you use scientific knowledge to build something useful, you become an inventor!
rounds.reflection_prompt: What other useful devices could you build using only mirrors and the law of reflection?
rounds.image_prompt: Student building a periscope from a cardboard tube with two small mirrors inside at 45 degrees, another student testing it by looking over a desk, excited expressions

choices.label: A. White light is actually a mixture of seven colors: violet, indigo, blue, green, yellow, orange, and red (VIBGYOR)
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ Isaac Newton discovered that white light is a mixture of seven colors. When white light passes through a prism, each color bends by a different amount (violet bends the most, red the least), spreading them into a beautiful rainbow spectrum. This is called dispersion! Rainbows form in the sky because raindrops act like tiny prisms.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Planning your approach carefully is a sign of strategic reasoning.

choices.label: B. White light is the purest form of light with no colors mixed in
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 Before Newton's famous prism experiment, people believed white light was pure. But Newton proved the opposite — white light is actually a MIXTURE of all the colors of the visible spectrum! When you pass white light through a prism, it splits into VIBGYOR. When you recombine all these colors, you get white light back!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Thinking ahead about consequences shows strategic planning ability.

choices.label: C. A prism adds color to white light by painting the light beam
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 A prism does NOT add any color to light. The colors are already there inside white light! The prism simply separates them because each color bends by a different amount as it passes through the glass. Violet bends the most and red bends the least. Newton proved this by using a second prism to recombine the colors back into white light.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Considering long-term impact before acting builds strategic thinking.

choices.label: D. Rainbows are caused by the Sun painting colors directly onto clouds
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 Rainbows form when sunlight enters millions of tiny water droplets in the air. Each droplet acts like a miniature prism — it refracts (bends) white light, splits it into its component colors, and reflects it back toward your eyes. The colors are always in the same order: red on top, violet at the bottom!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Weighing multiple outcomes before deciding strengthens your planning skills.

rounds.round_title: Week 10: Light & Heat — The Energy Connection
rounds.situation: Dr. Prism places a thermometer under a bright lamp. The temperature rises! 'Light carries energy,' she explains. 'Dark colors absorb more light energy and get hotter. That is why you feel warmer in a black shirt on a sunny day.' She sets out white and black paper, a lamp, and thermometers. Dev is excited about precise temperature measurements while Aisha wonders if you could cook with sunlight.
rounds.goal: Understand the relationship between light, color, and heat absorption.
rounds.coaching_moment: Risk tolerance: Testing bold ideas (like solar cooking!) requires willingness to try things that might not work. The best scientists are brave experimenters.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Why are most solar panels dark-colored? How does this connect to what you learned today?
rounds.image_prompt: Two pieces of paper (black and white) under a bright lamp with thermometers on each, student recording temperatures, clear temperature difference on displays

choices.label: A. Optical fibers carry internet signals using total internal reflection — light bounces inside the glass cable
choices.learning_concept: Applications of Light in Daily Life
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ Optical fibers use a phenomenon called total internal reflection, where light bouncing inside the glass fiber at a steep angle gets completely reflected and stays trapped inside. This allows light signals to travel thousands of kilometers through thin glass cables at incredible speeds — carrying your internet, phone calls, and streaming videos!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Looking beyond the obvious choice shows you think strategically.

choices.label: B. A magnifying glass cools things down by spreading sunlight over a wider area
choices.learning_concept: Applications of Light in Daily Life
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 A magnifying glass (convex lens) actually does the OPPOSITE — it CONCENTRATES sunlight into a tiny bright spot, making it intensely hot! That is why you should never leave a magnifying glass in direct sunlight on paper — it can start a fire. The lens focuses all the light energy from a large area into one small point.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Planning your approach carefully is a sign of strategic reasoning.

choices.label: C. Periscopes in submarines use refraction to see above the water surface
choices.learning_concept: Applications of Light in Daily Life
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 Periscopes use REFLECTION, not refraction. A periscope has two mirrors placed at 45-degree angles inside a tube. Light from above enters the top mirror, bounces down to the bottom mirror, and then into your eyes. The light bounces (reflects) off the mirrors — it does not pass through them.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Thinking ahead about consequences shows strategic planning ability.

choices.label: D. Dark-colored clothes keep you cooler in summer because they reflect more sunlight
choices.learning_concept: Applications of Light in Daily Life
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 It is actually the OPPOSITE! Dark colors ABSORB more light and heat, making you warmer. Light colors (especially white) REFLECT more sunlight and keep you cooler. That is why people in hot desert regions often wear white or light-colored clothes, and why rooftops in hot countries are painted white!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Considering long-term impact before acting builds strategic thinking.

rounds.situation: Dr. Prism's favorite topic! She holds up a glass prism and shines white light through it. A beautiful rainbow spectrum splashes across the wall — red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet! 'Isaac Newton proved that white light is a mixture of ALL colors,' she says proudly. 'Today you will split light into colors and then PUT THEM BACK TOGETHER!' Aisha gasps. Dev is already drawing the spectrum order. The whole class is mesmerized.
rounds.goal: Understand light dispersion through prisms and the visible spectrum.
rounds.coaching_moment: Empathy: Great teams leverage everyone's strengths. The best color experiments come from teams where every member feels valued and contributes ideas.
rounds.reflection_prompt: How does a prism separate white light into colors? Why does each color bend by a different amount?
rounds.image_prompt: Glass prism on lab bench splitting a beam of white light into a vivid rainbow spectrum on the white wall, students watching in awe, dark room with dramatic lighting

choices.label: A. When red, green, and blue lights are mixed together, they produce white light
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ Red, green, and blue are the three primary colors of light. When you mix all three at full intensity, they create white light — this is called additive color mixing. TV screens, phone displays, and computer monitors use millions of tiny red, green, and blue (RGB) sub-pixels to create every color you see on screen!

skill_explanation.creativity: Exploring an unconventional approach shows creative thinking.

choices.label: B. Mixing red and green light together makes brown light
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 Mixing red and green PAINT makes brown, but mixing red and green LIGHT makes YELLOW! Light mixing (additive) is completely different from paint mixing (subtractive). Red + green light = yellow; red + blue light = magenta; blue + green light = cyan. Mixing all three makes white — not brown or black!

skill_explanation.creativity: Looking at the problem from a new angle demonstrates creativity.

choices.label: C. A red apple looks red because it produces red light from inside
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 A red apple does NOT produce its own light — it is not luminous! It looks red because it ABSORBS all other colors of white light (green, blue, yellow, etc.) and REFLECTS only the red light back to your eyes. In a room lit only with green light, a red apple would actually look almost black!

skill_explanation.creativity: Combining ideas in unexpected ways shows innovative thinking.

choices.label: D. In a prism, red light bends the most and violet light bends the least
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 It is the other way around! VIOLET light bends the MOST and RED light bends the LEAST when passing through a prism. This is because violet light has a shorter wavelength and higher frequency, causing it to slow down more in glass. That is why violet is always at the bottom of a rainbow and red at the top!

skill_explanation.creativity: Not settling for the obvious solution builds creative problem-solving.

rounds.situation: CRISIS! A major storm has knocked out the school's electricity! The optics lab is pitch dark — no electric lamps, no ray boxes, no overhead lights. Only dim emergency lighting is working. The Science Fair is just two weeks away and your project needs finishing! Dr. Prism looks out at the grey sky and says: 'Well, scientists have worked without electricity for thousands of years. What can we do with only natural light and candles?'
rounds.goal: Keep your learning and Science Fair preparation going despite having no electricity.
rounds.coaching_moment: Resilience: The greatest innovations often come from constraints. When resources are limited, creativity and teamwork become your most powerful tools.
rounds.reflection_prompt: How did scientists like Isaac Newton study light before electricity was invented? What can we learn from them?
rounds.image_prompt: Dark school lab lit only by candles and window light, students working on optics experiments using natural light, creative atmosphere, storm visible through windows

choices.label: A. A solar eclipse happens when the Moon comes between the Sun and Earth, blocking sunlight
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ During a solar eclipse, the Moon passes directly between the Sun and Earth. The Moon's shadow falls on Earth, blocking the Sun's light for observers in that shadow. It is like a giant shadow experiment in space! The Moon is 400 times smaller than the Sun but also 400 times closer, so they appear almost the same size in our sky — a remarkable coincidence!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Weighing multiple outcomes before deciding strengthens your planning skills.

choices.label: B. A solar eclipse happens when Earth comes between the Sun and the Moon
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 When Earth comes between the Sun and Moon, that is a LUNAR eclipse, not a solar eclipse! In a lunar eclipse, Earth's shadow falls on the Moon, making it look reddish. In a SOLAR eclipse, the MOON comes between the Sun and Earth, casting its shadow on Earth. The names tell you which object goes dark — solar = Sun goes dark, lunar = Moon goes dark.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Looking beyond the obvious choice shows you think strategically.

choices.label: C. Eclipses happen every month because the Moon orbits Earth once a month
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 Although the Moon orbits Earth roughly every 29 days, eclipses do NOT happen every month. This is because the Moon's orbit is tilted about 5 degrees compared to Earth's orbit around the Sun. Most months, the Moon passes slightly above or below the direct line between Sun and Earth. Eclipses only happen when everything lines up perfectly!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Planning your approach carefully is a sign of strategic reasoning.

choices.label: D. You can safely look directly at a solar eclipse with your bare eyes
choices.feedback: Not quite — and this is very important for your safety! 💡 You should NEVER look directly at the Sun, even during an eclipse! The Sun's intense light can permanently damage your retina (the light-sensitive layer at the back of your eye) in seconds. Always use special eclipse glasses or pinhole projectors to view a solar eclipse safely.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Thinking ahead about consequences shows strategic planning ability.

rounds.situation: Power is restored and the Science Fair is next week! Dr. Prism gives full creative freedom: 'Use everything you have learned about light — shadows, reflection, refraction, colors, lenses — to create the most stunning light art or invention you can imagine. Think beyond the textbook. What can light do that nobody in this class has tried yet?' The lab buzzes with final preparations and wild ideas.
rounds.goal: Push your creativity and optics knowledge to design an original light-based creation.
rounds.coaching_moment: Creativity: Innovation happens when you combine things in new ways. Every great invention started as a 'What if...?' question.
rounds.reflection_prompt: What is the most surprising thing you learned about light this semester? How could you use that in a new way?
rounds.image_prompt: Student sketching a creative light installation design in notebook, surrounded by prisms, mirrors, LEDs and colored filters, lightbulb moment, messy but brilliant workspace

choices.label: A. A periscope uses two plane mirrors at 45 degrees to let you see over walls or around corners
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ A periscope consists of two plane mirrors placed at 45-degree angles inside a tube. Light from the scene above enters the top, hits the first mirror, bounces down to the second mirror, and then redirects into your eyes. This clever application of the Law of Reflection allows submarine crews to see above the ocean surface while staying underwater!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Considering long-term impact before acting builds strategic thinking.

choices.label: B. Concave mirrors are used as rear-view mirrors in cars because they make objects appear larger
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 Car rear-view and side mirrors typically use CONVEX mirrors (not concave). Convex mirrors curve outward and show a wider field of view, so drivers can see more of the road behind them. The trade-off is that objects appear smaller and farther away — that is why side mirrors say 'Objects in mirror are closer than they appear.'

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Weighing multiple outcomes before deciding strengthens your planning skills.

choices.label: C. A kaleidoscope creates beautiful patterns using refraction through colored glass
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 A kaleidoscope creates its patterns using REFLECTION, not refraction. It has two or three mirrors arranged at angles inside a tube. Colored beads or glass pieces at one end are reflected multiple times by the mirrors, creating symmetrical, repeating patterns. Each time you rotate it, the beads shift and the pattern changes!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Looking beyond the obvious choice shows you think strategically.

choices.label: D. Diffuse reflection from rough surfaces does not follow the law of reflection
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 Diffuse reflection DOES follow the law of reflection — at each tiny point on the rough surface, the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection. But because a rough surface has bumps pointing in many directions, the reflected rays scatter in all directions. The LAW is always obeyed, but the overall effect looks scattered because the surface is uneven.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Planning your approach carefully is a sign of strategic reasoning.

rounds.situation: Science Fair day is here! The gym is filled with display boards, projects, and excited visitors — parents, teachers, younger students, and even a local newspaper reporter. Your light and optics project is set up, prisms catching the light, mirrors reflecting beams, and your display board telling the story of your journey. Dr. Prism says: 'This is your moment to shine — literally! Show the world what you have learned about light.' How will you present?
rounds.goal: Present your optics project at the Science Fair and make the most of the experience.
rounds.coaching_moment: Resilience: Public presentation takes courage. Whether you win or not, sharing your work with confidence is itself a huge achievement.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Looking back at Week 1, what would you tell your past self about light? How much have you grown?
rounds.image_prompt: School Science Fair in a gymnasium, students presenting optics projects with colorful light displays, prisms creating rainbows, parents and teachers visiting, trophy on display

choices.label: A. A rainbow forms because each raindrop acts like a tiny prism that refracts and disperses sunlight
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ A rainbow is nature's spectacular display of dispersion! Each raindrop acts like a miniature prism — sunlight enters the drop, refracts (bends), reflects off the back surface inside the drop, and refracts again as it exits. Different colors bend by different amounts, so they separate into the full spectrum: red on the outside, violet on the inside.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Thinking ahead about consequences shows strategic planning ability.

choices.label: B. We can see a rainbow by looking directly toward the Sun during rain
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 To see a rainbow, you must have the Sun BEHIND you and the rain in FRONT of you. The sunlight enters the raindrops, gets dispersed, and bounces back toward you. If you face the Sun, you will never see a rainbow (plus it is dangerous to look at the Sun!). Rainbows always appear in the part of the sky OPPOSITE to the Sun.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Considering long-term impact before acting builds strategic thinking.

choices.label: C. Light always travels at the same speed regardless of the material it passes through
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 Light travels at different speeds in different materials — fastest in vacuum (~300,000 km/s), slightly slower in air, and noticeably slower in water and glass. This change in speed is exactly WHAT CAUSES refraction! If light traveled at the same speed everywhere, it would never bend, prisms would not create rainbows, and lenses would not work.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Weighing multiple outcomes before deciding strengthens your planning skills.

choices.label: D. A concave mirror and a convex lens both spread light rays apart
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 A concave mirror CONVERGES (focuses) light — just like a convex lens. And a convex mirror DIVERGES (spreads) light — just like a concave lens. The trick is: concave mirrors = convex lenses (both focus), and convex mirrors = concave lenses (both spread). Remember: 'cave' means it curves inward like a cave!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Looking beyond the obvious choice shows you think strategically.

glossary_terms.definition: A form of energy that travels in straight lines at incredibly high speed (300,000 km/s). It allows us to see objects and is part of the electromagnetic spectrum.
An object that produces its own light, such as the Sun, a torch, a candle flame, or an LED bulb.
An object that does not produce its own light but can be seen because it reflects light from a luminous source. Examples: the Moon, a book, a wall.
A dark area formed when an opaque object blocks light. Shadows prove that light travels in straight lines (rectilinear propagation).
The bouncing of light off a surface. The law of reflection states that the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection.
The bending of light when it passes from one medium to another (like air to water or air to glass). This happens because light changes speed in different materials.
A transparent curved piece of glass or plastic that bends light to focus or spread it. Convex lenses focus light; concave lenses spread it.
A triangular piece of glass that separates white light into its component colors (the visible spectrum) through dispersion.
The band of colors produced when white light is split by a prism: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, and violet (ROYGBIV).
A material that allows light to pass through it clearly so that objects behind it can be distinctly seen. Example: clear glass, clean water.
A material that allows some light to pass through but scatters it, so objects behind it appear blurred. Example: frosted glass, wax paper.
A material that does not allow any light to pass through it. It blocks light completely and creates a shadow. Example: wood, metal, cardboard.

endings.title: Master Optician
endings.message: You have achieved mastery in the Light & Shadow Lab! Your knowledge of optics is extraordinary, your safety record is impeccable, and your innovative light displays have inspired the entire school. Dr. Prism nominates you for the District Science Award, and the local newspaper features your Science Fair project on the front page. You have proven that curiosity, hard work, and creativity can illuminate the world — literally!

endings.title: Skilled Light Experimenter
endings.message: You have become a skilled optics experimenter with solid knowledge and good lab practices! Your Science Fair project demonstrates real competence in understanding light behavior. Dr. Prism is proud of your progress and says you are ready for the advanced physics elective next year. Your skills are genuine and your future in science is bright — pun intended!

endings.title: Lab Regular
endings.message: You completed the Light & Shadow Lab program with mixed results. Some weeks were great and others were tough, but you stuck with it and learned the basics of light and optics. Dr. Prism says there is always next semester to improve, and the foundation you built will serve you well. Keep experimenting — every expert was once a beginner!

endings.title: Struggling Student
endings.message: The Light & Shadow Lab was a tough journey for you. Many of the optics concepts were confusing, and the experiments did not always go as planned. But here is the important thing — you did not give up. Dr. Prism arranges extra tutoring sessions for you and says: 'The students who struggle the most often end up understanding the deepest, because they had to fight for every insight.' Your story is not over!

endings.title: Lab Probation
endings.message: Due to repeated safety violations — looking directly at bright lights, handling hot lenses carelessly, and ignoring goggle rules — Dr. Prism has placed you on Lab Probation. You can only observe experiments until you pass the safety certification test. Safety around light is non-negotiable — bright light can permanently damage eyes. Lumina has volunteered to tutor you personally. This setback is temporary — learn from it and come back stronger!
